topic: How PostgreSQL 17 incremental backups work (pg_basebackup --incremental, WAL summarization, pg_combinebackup) and their limitations

key_points.point: PostgreSQL 17 (released 2024-09-26) added incremental file-system backups via pg_basebackup --incremental plus the new pg_combinebackup tool and WAL summarization.
The server tracks changed blocks through WAL summary files, which record block numbers modified within an LSN range; they are produced by the WAL summarizer and kept under pg_wal/summaries.
summarize_wal is off by default and must be enabled (it cannot run with wal_level=minimal); without it incremental backups cannot be taken.
wal_summary_keep_time defaults to 10 days; summaries must cover the whole LSN range since the prior backup or the incremental fails, so set it above the gap between dependent backups.
pg_basebackup --incremental takes the backup_manifest of a prior backup from the same server; it uploads it, and the server sends only blocks changed since then (server version 17+ only).
Incremental backups replace some relation files with incremental files holding only changed blocks plus reconstruction metadata; non-relation files are copied in full.

An incremental backup cannot be restored directly: pg_combinebackup must merge the full backup and all intermediate incrementals, listed oldest to newest, into a synthetic full backup with -o, then normal recovery follows.

PostgreSQL does not track backup dependencies; deleting any backup in the chain makes later incrementals unrestorable, and pg_combinebackup validates chain relationships but not data integrity (use pg_verifybackup).
pg_combinebackup does not recompute page checksums: if checksum state changed between backups in the chain, output may hold invalid checksums; take a new full backup after changing checksums.
pg_combinebackup copy modes: default --copy; --clone (reflinks, Linux Btrfs/XFS, macOS APFS) and --copy-file-range can speed up reconstruction and save space where the filesystem supports them.
Incremental backups from a standby can fail with little activity since the previous backup (replay starts at the last restartpoint); the prior backup must also be on a compatible timeline.

Incremental backups mainly benefit large databases with mostly unchanged data; WAL archiving and recovery are still required, and for small or heavily modified databases full backups are simpler and similarly sized.
